claim: Two awake male rhesus monkeys were used for the electrophysiological recordings.
source: Two awake male rhesus monkeys were used for the electrophysiological recordings reported in this study.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Materials and methods section of the manuscript.

claim: Monkeys were implanted with a head holder and recording chambers above V1 under general anesthesia and sterile conditions.
source: After initial training, monkeys were implanted with a head holder and recording chambers above V1 under general anesthesia and sterile conditions (for details of surgical procedures, postsurgical analgesics, and general postsurgical treatment, see Thiele et al., 2006).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All procedures complied with the European Communities Council Directive RL 2010/63/EC, the U.S. National Institutes of Health Guidelines for the Care and Use of Animals for Experimental Procedures, and the UK Animals Scientific Procedures Act.
source: All procedures complied with the European Communities Council Directive RL 2010/63/EC, the U.S. National Institutes of Health Guidelines for the Care and Use of Animals for Experimental Procedures, and the UK Animals Scientific Procedures Act.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Recordings were performed using a 16-contact microelectrode (V-probe, Plexon, Dallas, Tex., US).
source: Recordings were performed using a 16-contact microelectrode (V-probe, Plexon, Dallas, Tex., US).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Contacts were arranged vertically along the electrode with an inter-contact spacing of 150 µm.
source: Contacts were arranged vertically along the electrode with an inter-contact spacing of 150 µm.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The raw signal of each electrode contact was recorded with 24 bits resolution at a sampling rate of 32 kHz.
source: The raw signal of each electrode contact was referenced to the guide tube and recorded with 24 bits resolution at a sampling rate of 32 kHz.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The LFP reflects the low-frequency changes of post-synaptic potentials.
source: It is assumed that the LFP reflects the low-frequency changes of post-synaptic potentials (Mitzdorf, 1987), while MUAe captures the aggregate high-frequency spiking activity of the population of neurons around the electrode contact (Supèr and Roelfsema, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations.

claim: MUAe captures the aggregate high-frequency spiking activity of the population of neurons around the electrode contact.
source: It is assumed that the LFP reflects the low-frequency changes of post-synaptic potentials (Mitzdorf, 1987), while MUAe captures the aggregate high-frequency spiking activity of the population of neurons around the electrode contact (Supèr and Roelfsema, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by citations.

claim: Small stimuli elicited gamma frequency oscillations predominantly in the superficial layers.
source: Small stimuli elicited gamma frequency oscillations predominantly in the superficial layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: Gamma oscillations from small stimuli Granger-causally originated in upper layer 4 and lower supragranular layers.
source: These Granger-causally originated in upper layer 4 and lower supragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: Large stimuli generated strong narrow band gamma oscillatory activity across cortical layers.
source: Unexpectedly, large stimuli generated strong narrow band gamma oscillatory activity across cortical layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: Gamma oscillations from large stimuli Granger-causally arose in layer 5.
source: They Granger-causally arose in layer 5, were conveyed through layer six to superficial layers, and violated existing models of feedback spectral signatures.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: Gamma oscillations from large stimuli were conveyed through layer six to superficial layers.
source: They Granger-causally arose in layer 5, were conveyed through layer six to superficial layers, and violated existing models of feedback spectral signatures.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: Large stimuli gamma oscillations violated existing models of feedback spectral signatures.
source: They Granger-causally arose in layer 5, were conveyed through layer six to superficial layers, and violated existing models of feedback spectral signatures.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: With large stimuli, alpha band oscillatory activity arose predominantly in granular and supragranular layers.
source: Equally surprising, with large stimuli, alpha band oscillatory activity arose predominantly in granular and supragranular layers and communicated in a feedforward direction.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: With large stimuli, alpha band oscillatory activity communicated in a feedforward direction.
source: Equally surprising, with large stimuli, alpha band oscillatory activity arose predominantly in granular and supragranular layers and communicated in a feedforward direction.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract.

claim: Feedforward inputs predominantly terminate in layer 4 of sensory cortical areas.
source: Feedforward inputs predominantly terminate in layer 4 of sensory cortical areas, before being passed to layers 2/3 and then onwards to layers 5/6, where recurrent inputs to layer 2/3 arise (Callaway, 1998; Callaway, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Feedback connections from downstream areas predominantly terminate in layer 1 and 5.
source: Conversely, feedback connections from downstream areas predominantly terminate in layer 1 and 5 (Rockland and Pandya, 1979), from where the information is passed to layers 2/3.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The earliest activity elicited by stimuli centered on the classical receptive field occurs in layer 4c.
source: Current source density analysis of the LFP, as well as latency of spiking activity has demonstrated that the earliest activity elicited by stimuli centered on the classical receptive field occurs in layer 4c (Bijanzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Stimuli restricted to the far receptive field surround initially activate V1 in upper superficial layers and in layer 5.
source: Stimuli restricted to the far receptive field surround, which are hypothesized to affect processing in V1 primarily through feedback projections (Bair et al., 2003), initially activate V1 in upper superficial layers and in layer 5 (Bijanzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Feedback processing has been aligned with low frequency (alpha band) oscillatory activity, dominating activity in infragranular layers.
source: Feedback processing has been aligned with low frequency (alpha [α] band) oscillatory activity, dominating activity in infragranular layers (Buffalo et al., 2011; Lopes Da Silva and Storm Van Leeuwen, 1977; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014), and with beta (β) band oscillations (Bastos et al., 2015a; Xing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Feedforward processing has been associated with low frequency theta, and higher frequency oscillatory activity (gamma band), originating in layer 4, dominating in supragranular layers.
source: Conversely, feedforward processing has been associated with low frequency theta [θ], and higher frequency oscillatory activity (gamma [γ] band), originating in layer 4, dominating in (or even being largely restricted to) supragranular layers (Bastos et al., 2015a; Bollimunta et al., 2011; Buffalo et al., 2004; Buffalo et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2010; Spaak et al., 2012; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014; Xing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The generality of the scenario that feedback is associated with low frequency oscillations in infragranular layers has been questioned.
source: However, the generality of this scenario has recently been questioned (Haegens et al., 2015), whereby the strongest low-frequency (α) oscillations generators were found in supragranular layers of sensory cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Most studies failed to find prominent gamma oscillations outside supragranular layers.
source: Moreover, while most studies failed to find prominent γ oscillations outside supragranular layers (Buffalo et al., 2011; Maier et al., 2010; Xing et al., 2012), exceptions do exist (Maier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Increasing the stimulus size invokes center surround interactions.
source: Increasing the stimulus size invokes center surround interactions, which result in specific input patterns across a cortical column (Bijanzadeh et al., 2018), and which strongly alter the spectral signatures LFPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Increasing the size of a patch of an orientated grating centered on a receptive field increases gamma power in conjunction with a general decrease of neurons firing rate.
source: Increasing the size of a patch of an orientated grating centered on a receptive field (RF) increases γ power in conjunction with a general decrease of neurons firing rate (Bauer et al., 1995; Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Jia et al., 2011; Ray and Maunsell, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by citations.

claim: 24 experiments from three hemispheres were included in the study after applying rejection criteria.
source: After applying the rejection criteria, we were left with 24 experiments (monkey 1: n = 17, monkey 2: n = 7) from three hemispheres which were included into this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The eighth channel from the top was defined as the alignment channel indicating putative layer 4c at zero depth in the example experiment.
source: In this recording the eighth channel from the top was defined as the alignment channel indicating putative layer 4c at zero depth (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The shortest latencies occurred in granular layers, followed by infragranular layers, with supragranular layers generally lagging behind.
source: The shortest latencies occurred in granular layers, followed by infragranular layers, with supragranular layers generally lagging behind (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Stimulus size significantly altered response latencies in granular layers (p < 0.01).
source: However, stimulus size significantly altered response latencies in granular (p < 0.01, one-factor-ANOVA, Figure 2C) and in infragranular layers (p < 0.001, one-factor-ANOVA, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Stimulus size significantly altered response latencies in infragranular layers (p < 0.001).
source: However, stimulus size significantly altered response latencies in granular (p < 0.01, one-factor-ANOVA, Figure 2C) and in infragranular layers (p < 0.001, one-factor-ANOVA, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In granular layers larger stimuli resulted in up to ~3ms longer latencies.
source: In granular layers larger stimuli resulted in up to ~3ms longer latencies, while in infragranular layers they caused up to ~6ms shorter latencies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: In infragranular layers larger stimuli caused up to ~6ms shorter latencies.
source: In granular layers larger stimuli resulted in up to ~3ms longer latencies, while in infragranular layers they caused up to ~6ms shorter latencies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: When large stimuli were presented the lag between granular and infragranular layers was reduced to ~2ms (from ~7ms for small stimuli).
source: Thus, when large stimuli were presented the lag between granular and infragranular layers was reduced to ~2ms (from ~7ms for small stimuli, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No significant changes in latency were found for supragranular layers (p = 0.98).
source: No significant changes were found for supragranular layers (p = 0.98, one-factor-ANOVA, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A current sink emerged ~75ms after stimulus onset at –600 µm when large stimuli were presented.
source: Specifically, a current sink emerged ~75ms after stimulus onset at –600 µm (Figure 2D and E), where a source was present when small stimuli were presented.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Stimulating the surround of a V1 RF results in additional input to infragranular layers.
source: This indicates that stimulating the surround of a V1 RF results in additional input to infragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Surround suppression affected all cortical layers.
source: Surround suppression affected all cortical layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Surround suppression was more pronounced in supragranular and granular than in infragranular layers.
source: However, it was more pronounced in supragranular and granular than in infragranular layers (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The stimulus size that resulted in maximal activity varied between layers.
source: Moreover, the stimulus size that resulted in maximal activity equally varied between layers, with slightly larger stimuli (0.75°, 1.5°) eliciting maximal activity in infragranular layers, while the smallest stimulus (0.5°) elicited maximal activity in supragranular layers (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stimuli extending into the far surround of neurons invoke center surround interactions through feedback connections from higher cortical areas that terminate predominantly in layers 1 and 5.
source: Together the results from Figures 2 and 3 are compatible with recent reports suggesting that stimuli extending into the far surround of neurons invoke center surround interactions through feedback connections from higher cortical areas that terminate predominantly in layers 1 and 5 (Bijanzadeh et al., 2018; Nassi et al., 2013; Nurminen et al., 2018; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: When small stimuli were presented, the supragranular layers showed relatively strong induced spectral power across multiple gamma frequencies (20–100 Hz).
source: When small stimuli were presented, the supragranular layers showed relatively strong iSP across multiple γ frequencies (20–100 Hz).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: When small stimuli were presented, there was weaker, but pronounced broad band induced spectral power (20–100 Hz) in infragranular layers.
source: In addition, there was weaker, but nevertheless pronounced broad band iSP (20–100 Hz) in infragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: As stimulus size increased the induced spectral power across all layers became more focused with clear peaks emerging in the low gamma frequency range (~40 Hz).
source: As stimulus size increased the iSP across all layers became more focused with clear peaks emerging in the low γ frequency range (~40 Hz).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Small stimuli (0.5°) elicit broad band power changes ranging from 30 to 100 Hz, with increasing induced spectral power toward higher frequencies in supragranular layers.
source: Small stimuli (0.5°) elicit broad band power changes ranging from 30 to 100 Hz, with increasing iSP toward higher frequencies in supragranular layers (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Infragranular layers showed relatively small, but homogenous broad band beta/gamma induced spectral power in the range from 20 to 80 Hz when small stimuli were shown.
source: Infragranular layers showed relatively small, but~ homogenous broad band β/γ iSP in the range from 20 to 80 Hz (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: When large stimuli were shown, induced spectral power in the supragranular layers concentrated in more narrow band regions of ~40 Hz.
source: When large stimuli were shown, iSP in the supragranular layers concentrated in more narrow band regions of ~40 Hz.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: A surprisingly large gamma frequency induced spectral power increase occurred in infragranular layers 5 and 6, at ~40–50 Hz when large stimuli were shown.
source: A surprisingly large γ frequency iSP increase occurred in infragranular layers 5 and 6, at ~40–50 Hz (compare to Xing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and compared to a citation.

claim: The peak frequency of the evoked gamma oscillation at around 40 Hz showed the same inverse relationship to stimulus size.
source: Also, the peak frequency of the evoked gamma oscillation at around 40 Hz showed the same inverse relationship to stimulus size (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008), and is in line with other previous publications using grating stimuli (Bauer et al., 1995; Gray et al., 1989; Jia et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: For theta-band, alpha-band, and beta-band, stimulus-size-induced changes are most pronounced for granular and lower supragranular layers.
source: For the θ-band, α-band, and β-band, stimulus-size-induced changes are most pronounced for granular and lower supragranular layers (Figure 5C, F 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: For infragranular layers, larger stimuli caused a reduction in theta-band.
source: For infragranular layers, larger stimuli caused a reduction in θ-band (Figure 5B), no change in α-band or β-band, and strong increases in γ-band.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For infragranular layers, larger stimuli caused no change in alpha-band or beta-band.
source: For infragranular layers, larger stimuli caused a reduction in θ-band (Figure 5B), no change in α-band or β-band, and strong increases in γ-band.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: For infragranular layers, larger stimuli caused strong increases in gamma-band.
source: For infragranular layers, larger stimuli caused a reduction in θ-band (Figure 5B), no change in α-band or β-band, and strong increases in γ-band.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Larger stimuli caused significantly more gamma-band across all contacts.
source: Overall, larger stimuli caused significantly more γ-band across all contacts (Figure 5J), but relative changes are strongest in supragranular and infragranular layers (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Relative changes in gamma-band are strongest in supragranular and infragranular layers.
source: Overall, larger stimuli caused significantly more γ-band across all contacts (Figure 5J), but relative changes are strongest in supragranular and infragranular layers (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Alpha-oscillations locked to the alpha-phase in granular layers appeared to originate in infragranular and upper supragranular layers, progressing toward middle supragranular layers.
source: Specifically, it was shown that α-oscillations locked to the α-phase in granular layers appeared to originate in infragranular and upper supragranular layers, progressing toward middle supragranular layers (van Kerkoerle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Gamma-oscillations locked to the gamma-phase in granular layers originated in granular or lower supragranular layer progressing toward upper supragranular and infragranular layers respectively.
source: Conversely, γ-oscillations locked to the γ -phase in granular layers originated in granular or lower supragranular layer progressing toward upper supragranular and infragranular layers respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Low frequency (theta, alpha) showed a phase progression from layer 5 to layer 6, and then to granular and supragranular layers for small stimuli.
source: Low frequency (θ, α) showed a phase progression from layer 5 to layer 6, and then to granular and supragranular layers for small stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: For larger stimuli, low frequency (theta, alpha) phase progression was seen bidirectionally from granular to supragranular and to infragranular layer 5, but also from infragranular layer 6 to layer 5.
source: This pattern changed radically for larger stimuli, where phase progression was seen bidirectionally from granular to supragranular and to infragranular layer 5, but also from infragranular layer 6 to layer 5.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: For gamma frequencies, layer 4 and 6 were largely in phase for small stimuli, but almost 90° out of phase with layer 5.
source: For γ frequencies, layer 4 and 6 were largely in phase for small stimuli, but almost 90° out of phase with layer 5.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: For large stimuli, gamma frequency phase progression occurred from layer 5 to layer 6, onwards to granular layers, and then to supragranular layers.
source: However, for large stimuli phase progression occurred from layer 5 to layer 6, onwards to granular layers, and then to supragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: A striking feature of the directionality of all Granger causalities (irrespective of the frequency bands analyzed) was its dominance in the 'upward' direction, namely toward supragranular layers.
source: A striking feature of the directionality of all GCs (irrespective of the frequency bands analyzed) was its dominance in the 'upward' direction, namely toward supragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Communication was directed toward the cortico-cortical feedforward channels in V1.
source: This indicates that communication was directed toward the cortico-cortical feedforward channels in V1 (for related results see Ferro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Sizeable Granger causalities in the downward direction were usually restricted to granular to infragranular interactions, and to layer 5 to layer 6 interactions.
source: Sizeable GCs in the downward direction were usually restricted to granular to infragranular interactions, and to layer 5 to layer 6 interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Downward Granger causalities were generally more pronounced with larger stimuli.
source: Downward GCs were generally more pronounced with larger stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Strong theta-Granger causalities originated in layer 6 (lower contacts) affecting predominantly supragranular layers, irrespective of stimulus size.
source: In the upward direction strong θ-GCs originated in layer 6 (lower contacts) affecting predominantly supragranular layers, irrespective of stimulus size.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: With increasing stimulus size, theta-Granger causalities increased in an upward direction between granular and supragranular, and between supragranular-supragranular contacts.
source: With increasing stimulus size GCs increased in an upward direction between granular and supragranular, and between supragranular-supragranular contacts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: A very similar pattern to theta was present for Granger causalities in the alpha-frequency band.
source: Overall, a very similar pattern was present for GCs in the α- frequency band.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: In the beta-frequency band, Granger causalities were fairly weak in the downward direction when small stimuli were presented, but increased between layer 5 and layer 6 for large stimuli.
source: In the β- frequency band, GCs were fairly weak in the downward direction, when small stimuli were presented, but increased between layer 5 and layer 6 for large stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Upward beta-frequency Granger causalities were pronounced between granular and supragranular, and between supra-supragranular contacts for all stimulus sizes.
source: Upward GCs were pronounced between granular and supragranular, and between supra-supragranular contacts for all stimulus sizes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: With increase in stimulus size a pronounced infragranular-supragranular beta-frequency Granger causality occurred.
source: With increase in stimulus size a pronounced infragranular-supragranular GC occurred.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: An overall similar pattern to beta was present for gamma-frequency Granger causalities, with an even stronger increase in upwards directed supra-supragranular Granger causalities with stimulus size.
source: An overall similar pattern was present for γ-frequency GCs, with an even stronger increase in upwards directed supra-supragranular GCs with stimulus size.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Surround modulation results in strongly increased low, mid and high frequency band communication between granular and supragranular compartments.
source: The results from Figure 7 show that surround modulation results in strongly increased low, mid and high frequency band communication between granular and supragranular compartments, and it results in strongly increased γ-band communication originating from layer 5, which drives γ frequency changes in layer 6, and which in turn changes γ frequency oscillations in upper layer four and in layers 2/3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Surround modulation results in strongly increased gamma-band communication originating from layer 5, which drives gamma frequency changes in layer 6, and which in turn changes gamma frequency oscillations in upper layer four and in layers 2/3.
source: The results from Figure 7 show that surround modulation results in strongly increased low, mid and high frequency band communication between granular and supragranular compartments, and it results in strongly increased γ-band communication originating from layer 5, which drives γ frequency changes in layer 6, and which in turn changes γ frequency oscillations in upper layer four and in layers 2/3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Narrow band gamma frequency oscillations occur across cortical layers and increase across cortical layers with increasing stimulus size.
source: Using stimuli of different sizes in combination with laminar recordings in primary visual cortex of the macaque revealed that narrow band γ frequency oscillations occur across cortical layers and increase across cortical layers with increasing stimulus size.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: When stimuli encroached on the far surround of the receptive field, the LFP gamma oscillations in layer 5 exerted pronounced granger causal influences on gamma oscillations in layer 6.
source: When stimuli encroached on the far surround of the receptive field, the LFP γ oscillations in layer 5, the feedback recipient layer, exerted pronounced granger causal influences on γ oscillations in layer 6, which in turn granger causal influenced γ oscillations in supragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Gamma oscillations in layer 6 granger causal influenced gamma oscillations in supragranular layers.
source: When stimuli encroached on the far surround of the receptive field, the LFP γ oscillations in layer 5, the feedback recipient layer, exerted pronounced granger causal influences on γ oscillations in layer 6, which in turn granger causal influenced γ oscillations in supragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The pattern of gamma frequency granger causal interactions is compatible with the known anatomical termination sites of feedback connections into V1.
source: This pattern of γ frequency granger causal interactions is compatible with the known anatomical termination sites of feedback connections into V1 (Rockland and Pandya, 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: The flow of information (granger causal interactions in the gamma frequency range) occurred in a manner compatible with the canonical microcircuit, but in a largely reverse direction.
source: The flow of information (granger causal interactions in the γ frequency range) occurred in a manner compatible with the canonical microcircuit, but in a largely reverse direction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Gamma oscillations are neither restricted to superficial layers, nor are they invariably signatures of feedforward communication.
source: This demonstrates that γ oscillations are neither restricted to superficial layers, nor are they invariably signatures of feedforward communication.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Low-frequency oscillation Granger causality interactions did not strictly adhere to their proposed role in feedback communication.
source: Moreover, low-frequency oscillation GC interactions did not strictly adhere to their proposed role in feedback communication, showing most profound increases in granular to supragranular and supra- to supragranular interactions with stimulus size.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Feedback influence terminating in layer five was not dominated by low-frequency oscillations as predicted by recent publications.
source: Feedback influence terminating in layer five was not dominated by low-frequency oscillations as predicted by recent publications (Bastos et al., 2015a; Bastos et al., 2015b; Bosman et al., 2012; Buffalo et al., 2011; Buschman and Miller; van Kerkoerle et al., 2014), even though GC interactions in low-frequency bands in the intracolumnar feedback direction (infragranular to granular/supragranular layers) were profound (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Low-frequency oscillations are not restricted (or dominant) to infragranular layer and can attain feedforward roles in V1.
source: This demonstrates that low-frequency oscillations are not restricted (or dominant) to infragranular layer and can attain feedforward roles in V1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The earliest responses in V1 occurred in layer 4c, aligned with the earliest current sink.
source: In line with predictions from the anatomy (Callaway, 1998; Callaway, 2004; Lund, 1988), the earliest responses in V1 occurred in layer 4 c, aligned with the earliest current sink.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Responses in layer 4c were followed by responses in layer 6.
source: This was followed by responses in layer 6.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Responses in supragranular layers were delayed by up to 20ms.
source: Responses in supragranular layers were delayed by up to 20ms.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The early responses in layer six are likely mediated by direct inputs from the LGN.
source: The early responses in layer six are likely mediated by direct inputs from the LGN (Callaway, 1998; Callaway, 2004; Lund, 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Stimulus size affected response latencies in layer 4, where increasing stimulus size initially resulted in decreased latencies, probably due to increased excitatory drive, followed by increased latencies when stimuli were larger than 1.5°.
source: Stimulus size affected response latencies in layer 4, where increasing stimulus size initially resulted in decreased latencies, probably due to increased excitatory drive, followed by increased latencies when stimuli were larger than 1.5°.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The increase in latencies in layer 4 when stimuli were larger than 1.5° is most likely driven by surround suppression at the level of the LGN and the retina.
source: This increase is most likely driven by surround suppression at the level of the LGN and the retina (Alitto and Usrey, 2008; Bijanzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: In layers 5 and 6, increasing stimulus size resulted in shorter response latencies with an asymptote reached once stimuli were 1.5° in size.
source: In layers 5 and 6, increasing stimulus size resulted in shorter response latencies with an asymptote reached once stimuli were 1.5° in size.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The shorter response latencies in layers 5 and 6 with increasing stimulus size could be due to a mixture of increased excitation from LGN inputs, and fast feedback inputs that compensate for the surround suppression inherited from feedforward inputs when stimuli exceed 1.5°.
source: This could be due to a mixture of increased excitation from LGN inputs, and fast feedback inputs (Bair et al., 2002; Bijanzadeh et al., 2018) that compensate for the surround suppression inherited from feedforward inputs when stimuli exceed 1.5°.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Surround suppression was largely homogenous for supragranular and granular recording sites, but decreased notably for layers 5 and 6.
source: Surround suppression was largely homogenous for supragranular and granular recording sites, but decreased notably for layers 5 and 6.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The decreased surround suppression in layers 5 and 6 is speculated to be a consequence of the added feedback drive from higher cortical areas.
source: We speculate that the decreased surround suppression in layers 5 and 6 is a consequence of the added feedback drive (Angelucci et al., 2002; Bair et al., 2002; Bijanzadeh et al., 2018; Rockland and Pandya, 1979) from higher cortical areas.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: The strength of narrow band gamma frequency oscillations increased monotonically with stimulus size.
source: In line with previous studies, we show that the strength of narrow band γ frequency oscillations increased monotonically with stimulus size (Bauer et al., 1995; Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Jia et al., 2011; Peter et al., 2019; Ray and Maunsell, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: Gamma frequency power was largely broadband for small stimuli, and most profound in supragranular layers.
source: γ frequency power was largely broadband for small stimuli, and most profound in supragranular layers.
